content.text: The diagram shows a device connected to a meter. What device is shown in the diagram?

content.alt_text: A rectangular coil on a horizontal axis between the N pole of a magnet on the left and the S pole of a magnet on the right, spinning on a dashed axis, its ends connected by two slip rings to an analogue meter reading 0 to 2 below.

content.text: AC motor
DC motor
AC generator
DC generator
Ask two separate questions: is electrical energy being converted to mechanical energy (motor), or mechanical energy to electrical energy (generator)?

Then examine how the two ends of the coil reach the external circuit. Continuous rings pass the induced emf through unchanged, whereas two half-rings attached to the coil swap connections every half turn.
D

The coil turns in the field and cuts flux lines, so an emf is induced in the coil and a current flows through the meter. Mechanical energy is being converted to electrical energy, so the device is a generator, not a motor.

The enlarged part of the figure shows the two ends of the coil resting on two separate curved segments with a clear gap between them, contacted by brushes. That is a split-ring commutator, not a pair of slip rings. The commutator swaps the coil connections every half rotation, so the emf delivered to the external circuit is always in the same direction and the output is direct current.

A pair of slip rings would deliver the emf unchanged and it would reverse twice per cycle, giving an alternating output and an AC generator. The gap between the two segments is what distinguishes the commutator from slip rings in the figure.

content.text: What is currently used to define the standard metre?
The speed of light
The signals from GPS satellites
The wavelength of light from a krypton lamp

In the SI system the numerical values of a few quantities are fixed exactly by definition, and the other units are derived from them.
Consider which listed quantity is defined as an exact constant, and what the metre is therefore measured in terms of.

Since 1983 the metre has been defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time of $1/299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{s}$, that is, from the now exact value of the speed of light. The other options are obsolete or irrelevant definitions: the krypton-86 wavelength (1960) and the platinum-iridium bar (1889) were earlier standards, and GPS signals are used for navigation and timing, not to define the metre.

content.text: What part of a cathode ray tube allows a person to observe the position of an electron beam?
A maltese cross
A heated filament
A fluorescent screen
A uniform magnetic field
The electrons making up the cathode ray are themselves invisible.
Ask which component of the tube converts the energy of the arriving electrons into light, so that the position of the beam on it can be seen.
C

The cathode ray is a beam of electrons, so its position cannot be seen directly. Electrons striking a fluorescent screen (typically coated with zinc sulphide) transfer their kinetic energy to the coating, which re-emits it as visible light, so the screen shows where the beam is. The Maltese cross is used to show that the particles have mass, the heated filament releases the electrons, and a magnetic or electric field deflects the beam.

content.text: In moving-coil galvanometers, the coil experiences a torque because of the current flowing through it. What ensures that this torque is directly proportional to the current flowing through the coil?
A return spring
A radial magnetic field
A laminated soft iron core
A constant cross-sectional area of the coil
The torque on a current loop is $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$.
For $\tau$ to depend on $I$ alone, every other factor must stay constant at every deflection. Think about the angle between the field and the plane of the coil as the coil rotates.
B

The torque on a current loop is $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$. If the magnetic field is radial, the field is always perpendicular to the plane of the coil, so $\theta = 90^\circ$ and $\sin\theta = 1$ at all deflections. The area, number of turns and field strength are then constant, so the torque is directly proportional to $I$.

content.text: Compared to a geostationary orbit, which row of the table correctly describes the relative properties of a low Earth orbit?
Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D
Write $v_{\text{orb}} = \sqrt{GM/r}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^{3}/GM}$ and consider how each depends on $r$.
A low Earth orbit has a much smaller radius than a geostationary orbit. Use that to fix the direction of the change in each column before reading the table.
B
A low Earth orbit has $r \approx 7.0\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$ while a geostationary orbit has $r \approx 4.2\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m}$, so the low Earth orbit has the much smaller radius.

Orbital velocity: $v_{\mathrm{orb}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ falls as $r$ rises, so the low Earth orbit has the higher orbital velocity, about $7.7\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ compared with $3.1\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ for a geostationary orbit. This eliminates rows C and D.
Orbital period: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}}$ rises as $r^{3/2}$, so the low Earth orbit has the shorter period, about $90\,\mathrm{min}$ compared with $24\,\mathrm{h}$. This eliminates row A.
Higher orbital velocity together with a lower orbital period is row B.

content.text: Which of the following ideal transformers could be used to convert an input voltage of 20 volts AC to an output voltage of 2 volts AC?

content.alt_text: Ideal transformer with a 4 turn primary coil and a 10 turn secondary coil on a laminated core.
Ideal transformer with a 20 turn primary coil and a 3 turn secondary coil.
Ideal transformer with a 20 turn primary coil and a 10 turn secondary coil.
Ideal transformer with a 3 turn primary coil and a 30 turn secondary coil.

content.text: For an ideal transformer $V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s$, so the output voltage is fixed by the turns ratio alone.
Work out the ratio $N_s/N_p$ that turns 20 V into 2 V, then identify in each figure which coil is the 20 V input.
D

For an ideal transformer $V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s$, so the ratio of the turns alone fixes the output voltage. Converting $20\,\mathrm{V}$ to $2\,\mathrm{V}$ needs $V_s/V_p = 2/20 = 0.1$, that is $N_s/N_p = 0.1$: the input coil must carry ten times as many turns as the output coil.

Reading the four figures gives 4 and 10 turns (A), 20 and 3 (B), 20 and 10 (C) and 3 and 30 (D). Only D puts ten turns on the input side for every turn on the output side, so only D is a step-down of 10:1. Feeding the $20\,\mathrm{V}$ into D's 30 turn coil gives $V_s = 20 \times 3/30 = 2\,\mathrm{V}$; feeding it into the 3 turn coil instead would step the voltage up to $200\,\mathrm{V}$. No other pair works - A gives 8 V or 50 V, B gives 3 V or 133 V and C gives 10 V or 40 V, depending on which coil takes the input.
Option D is therefore the correct choice.

content.text: A magnet can be levitated above a superconductor, when the superconductor is below its critical temperature. Which statement best describes how this occurs?
All of the magnet's field is absorbed by the superconductor.
The superconductor creates currents in the magnet, resulting in a repulsive force.
Cooper pairs are exchanged between the superconductor and the magnet through its field.
Some of the magnet's field is excluded by the superconductor, resulting in a repulsive force.
Below its critical temperature a superconductor expels magnetic field from its bulk (the Meissner effect), which sets up currents in its surface layer.
Ask whether the interaction between those induced currents and the magnet is attractive or repulsive.
D

Below its critical temperature a superconductor expels magnetic flux from its bulk (the Meissner effect). Surface currents induced in the superconductor set up their own field that opposes the magnet's field within the superconductor, and the resulting force between the magnet and those currents is repulsive, allowing the magnet to levitate.

content.text: An ideal electric motor connected to a DC voltage source rotates at a constant rate of 200 revolutions per minute. There is no load on the motor. Which of the following is a correct statement about the operation of the motor?
The applied voltage must exceed the back emf in order to keep the motor running.
There is no back emf because it is only produced in AC motors due to the changing flux.
The back emf is equal to the applied voltage because no work is being done by the motor.
The back emf must exceed the applied voltage to prevent the motor's speed from increasing.
The question specifies an IDEAL motor with NO load, so consider where the energy from the supply goes.
Compare the applied voltage with the back emf: with no losses and no mechanical output, what must be true of the two?
C

Any rotating coil generates a back emf by electromagnetic induction, whatever supplies it, so there is a back emf in this DC motor (eliminating B). The back emf opposes the supply, so it can never exceed the applied voltage in a running motor (eliminating D).

For an ideal motor with no load there is no friction and no mechanical output, so no power is dissipated or delivered. The only opposition to the supply voltage is the back emf, hence the applied voltage must equal it: $V = \varepsilon_{\text{back}}$. This is option C.

Option A describes a real motor, where the applied voltage must exceed the back emf to drive the losses and provide torque. Here that is excluded by the words 'ideal' and 'no load'. This agrees with the official 2012 HSC Physics key (Q16 = C).

A semiconductor absorbs a photon only if the photon's energy is at least as large as its band gap.

content.text: Outline a first-hand investigation that could be performed to measure a value for acceleration due to gravity.

Whatever method you choose, the outline must state the quantities you will measure and the equation that connects them to $g$, and it must be a first-hand method. A pendulum works if you can measure length and period; free fall works if you can measure distance and time. This part is worth 1 mark, so a bare method is enough.

Set a pendulum bob of length $L$ swinging with small amplitude and time $N$ oscillations; repeat for several values of $L$ and graph $T^{2}$ against $L$. The gradient is $4\pi^{2}/g$, so $g = 4\pi^{2}/\text{gradient}$.

Hang a small dense bob on a long light inextensible string and measure the distance $L$ from the pivot to the centre of the bob with a metre rule. Displace the bob slightly and release it; with a light gate or stopwatch time $N$ complete oscillations and divide by $N$ to obtain the period $T$. Repeat the timing several times and average, then repeat for at least five values of $L$. Plot $T^{2}$ against $L$ to obtain a straight line whose gradient is $4\pi^{2}/g$, giving $g$.

items: 1 mark: coherent outline of a first-hand procedure that produces data allowing $g$ to be calculated (e.g. pendulum: measure $L$ and $T$, then $g = 4\pi^2L/T^{2}$; or free-fall with a ticker timer).

content.text: How would you assess the accuracy of the result of the investigation?

Accuracy is about closeness to the true value, not about scatter, so the answer needs a source for the accepted value and a number for the size of the difference, such as a percentage difference. Say which part of your method would cause a systematic error.
Compare the value obtained with the accepted value $9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and evaluate the percentage difference.

Compare the experimental value of $g$ with the accepted value of $9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ from a data source. If the percentage difference is small (a few per cent) the result is accurate. Systematic error from measuring the pivot-to-centre-of-bob length or from using a stopwatch is the main source of inaccuracy.

items: 1 mark: comparison of the measured value with a reliable secondary source (or accepted value) and a statement of the size of the difference/percentage error.

content.text: How would you increase the reliability of the data collected?

Reliability is about scatter between repeats, so the technique is to collect more data: repeat each measurement, and time many oscillations per trial rather than one, then average. Taking readings across a range of values of the independent variable is also what makes the analysis possible.
Repeat each measurement many times over a range of values of $L$ and average the results.

Perform several trials at each value of $L$, time many oscillations rather than one in each trial, and average the results. Collecting a large number of readings reduces the effect of random fluctuations.

items: 1 mark: identifies repetition (multiple trials, several sets of data) and averaging as the main way of improving reliability.

content.text: How would you assess the reliability of the data collected?

You need a numerical measure of the scatter: the range, the standard deviation, or half the difference between the highest and lowest repeat, calculated at a fixed value of the independent variable. Then state a judgement about whether it is small enough, and say how you would improve the results if it were not.

Examine the spread of the repeated measurements (e.g. the range or standard deviation). A small spread shows the data are reliable; a large spread shows they are not. Compare the spread with the size of the measured value to decide whether it is acceptable.

Calculate the range (or standard deviation) of the repeated values of $T$ at each value of $L$. Because the same procedure is repeated under the same conditions, random errors should be small. If the spread is small compared with the measured values the data are reliable; if the spread is comparable with the measured values the results are unreliable and the timing procedure should be improved, for example by timing more oscillations per trial.

content.text: Explain the reason for changes in the reading on the electronic balance as the solenoid is removed.
Use Lenz's law: the induced current sets up a field that opposes the change in flux which produced it.
The flux is decreasing as the solenoid is lifted off the magnet, so work out whether the solenoid is trying to pull the magnet back or push it away, and on which side of the magnet the solenoid is.

The reading is a force measurement, so ask what extra force the pan has to support. Then remember the reading returns to the true mass once the motion stops, since the effect exists only while the flux is changing.

The induced current flows in the direction that opposes the decrease in magnetic flux as the solenoid is lifted clear, so the solenoid attracts the magnet upwards towards it. The balance therefore supports less than the true weight, so the reading falls below $42.42\,\mathrm{g}$ while the solenoid is moving and returns to $42.42\,\mathrm{g}$ once the solenoid has been removed and the flux has stopped changing.

Apply Lenz's law to the change in flux. The solenoid is above the magnet and is being lifted away from it, so the flux threading the coil falls and the induced current flows in the direction that opposes that decrease. The coil's own field therefore pulls the magnet back towards the coil, and because the coil is above the magnet that force on the magnet is upwards. Note that it also opposes the motion of the solenoid, which is exactly what Lenz's law requires.

The effect is brief because it depends on the flux changing, not on the solenoid being nearby: once the solenoid is clear, $|\varepsilon| = N|\Delta\Phi/\Delta t|$ falls to zero, the induced current dies away and the reading returns to $42.42\,\mathrm{g}$, the true mass.

In the reverse motion, lowering the solenoid towards the magnet increases the flux, so the induced current opposes the approach and the solenoid repels the magnet downwards; the reading then rises while the solenoid moves and returns to $42.42\,\mathrm{g}$ when it stops. Either way the magnetic force opposes the motion, which is the same point as conservation of energy: the work the student does lifting the solenoid against the attraction is dissipated as heat in the short-circuited wire.

content.text: Explain the motion of each of the masses after their release.
The towers are as tall as a geostationary satellite, so the field strength at the top of each tower is $g = GM/r^{2}$ evaluated at a much larger radius than at the surface.
Each mass is released from rest relative to its tower, not relative to the centre of the Earth. Work out the sideways velocity each mass has at the moment of release.

Compare that sideways velocity for a point on the rotation axis with that for a point on the equator, remembering that points on the equator sweep out the largest circle in the same time, $v = 2\pi r/T$.

Both masses fall towards the centre of the Earth with an acceleration less than $g$ because the field is weaker at 36 000 km altitude. The mass from Tower A has no initial sideways velocity and falls straight down. The mass from Tower B already has a tangential velocity of about 465 m/s from Earth's rotation, so it follows a curved, elliptical (orbit-like) path and lands some distance from the base of Tower B; it takes longer to reach the ground than the mass from Tower A.

At a geostationary altitude of about 36 000 km the field strength is $g = GM/r^{2}$, which is much smaller than at the surface, so both masses accelerate inwards slowly along approximately elliptical orbits with the release point as apogee. Neither mass is given the horizontal speed of about 3.1 km/s needed for a circular orbit, so neither mass orbits. The mass released from Tower A has zero velocity relative to Earth's axis, so it falls vertically down a meridian towards the North Pole. The mass released from Tower B keeps the tangential velocity of the rotating Earth at the equator (about 465 m/s), so its path is curved, and it lands well away from the base of the tower. Because the field is weakest at the release point, both masses take longer to reach the surface than they would under a constant $9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ field.

content.text: Using a labelled diagram, outline the differences in the energy bands of conductors, semiconductors and insulators.
Draw three separate diagrams, each with an energy axis, a conduction band at the top and a valence band below it, and label both bands in every diagram.
What distinguishes the three cases is how full the valence band is and how the gap between the bands compares with the thermal energy of the electrons at ordinary temperatures.

Conductors: partially filled conduction band, or overlapping valence and conduction bands. Semiconductors: filled valence band separated from an empty conduction band by a small energy gap (about 1 eV). Insulators: filled valence band separated from an empty conduction band by a large energy gap.

For an insulator the gap is large (order $10\,\mathrm{eV}$ or more), so thermal energy cannot normally promote electrons across it.

content.text: Explain why a current is able to flow in a pure semiconductor when an electric field is applied across it.
A completely full valence band cannot contribute to a current, so ask what has to happen for electrons to reach the empty conduction band.
Thermal energy is enough to move a few electrons across a small gap. Consider what is left behind when an electron leaves a filled band, and how that vacancy travels when a field is applied.

Thermal energy promotes a small number of electrons from the full valence band into the empty conduction band, leaving holes. The applied field accelerates conduction electrons against the field and the holes (valence electrons) with it, so both contribute to a net current.

In a pure semiconductor at ordinary temperatures a small fraction of valence-band electrons are promoted thermally into the conduction band, leaving an equal number of vacancies, or holes. When a field is applied the conduction electrons accelerate in the direction opposite to the field while the valence-band electrons move to fill the holes, so the holes appear to move in the direction of the field. The drift of both types of charge carrier constitutes a small current; doping greatly increases the number of carriers and hence the current.

content.text: Why have transistor circuits largely replaced thermionic devices?
Compare the two devices feature by feature: physical size, mass, cost, power consumption, start-up time, reliability and working life.
One of those properties also explains the most important change of all, namely that thousands or millions of the devices can now be fabricated on a single chip.

Transistors are much smaller, lighter, cheaper, use far less power, have no warm-up time, are more reliable and last longer than thermionic valves, and many can be fabricated on a single integrated circuit.

A thermionic valve contains a heated filament, a grid and a second electrode, so it is bulky, consumes significant power to heat the filament, needs time to warm up, ages and burns out, and only one function can be performed per valve. A transistor performs the same function at very small size and power, starts instantly, is reliable and cheap in large quantities, and many transistors can be fabricated on a single integrated circuit chip.

Positively, transistors made devices dramatically smaller, cheaper, faster and more reliable than valves. content.text: A transmission line is to be used to supply 100 MW of power from a power station to a substation 100 km away. Three possible designs are shown below.

content.alt_text: Design A, low voltage: a power station with 120 MW output feeding two 33 kV pylons across a 100 km line to a substation taking 100 MW input at 33 kV.
Design B, high voltage: a power station with step-up transformer and 508 kV output feeding two pylons with 40 ohm total line resistance across 100 km to a substation taking 100 MW input at 500 kV.
Design C, superconducting: a power station feeding a superconducting transmission line 100 km long, cooled by refrigeration units, to a substation taking 100 MW input.

content.text: Using physics principles and appropriate calculations, evaluate each design to determine the best way of transmitting power from the power station to the substation.
For each design extract the transmission voltage and any line resistance from the diagram, then use $P = VI$ for the line current and $P_{loss} = I^{2}R$ for the energy lost in the conductors.
Start with Design A. Working out the current needed to carry 100 MW at 33 kV shows why a low transmission voltage is impractical, whatever the line resistance turns out to be.

For Design C, separate the loss in the line itself from the power consumed by the refrigeration, and add them before comparing efficiencies. Then weigh the energy figures against capital cost and practicality.
Design B is the best design: loss 1.6 MW (98.4% efficient). Design C is a close second with no line loss but 3.0 MW consumed by cooling. Design A is worst, carrying 3.0 kA.

Design A carries 100 MW at 33 kV, so $I = P/V = 1.0 \times 10^{8}/3.3 \times 10^{4} = 3.0 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{A}$. Since the loss in the conductors is $P = I^2R$ and $I$ is so large, the loss in Design A would be enormous for any practical line resistance, and the conductors would have to be very heavy.

Design B: $I = 1.0 \times 10^{8}/5.0 \times 10^{5} = 200\,\mathrm{A}$. $P_{loss} = I^2R = (200)^{2} \times 40 = 1.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{W}$ = 1.6 MW, an efficiency of $100/101.6 = 98.4\%$. Only 20% more power is generated than is delivered.

Design C: the superconducting line has essentially no resistive loss, but the refrigeration consumes $30\,\mathrm{kW}$ per km, so for 100 km the overhead is $3.0\,\mathrm{MW}$ (efficiency 97.1%), together with very high capital cost and the engineering difficulty of maintaining a superconductor.

On energy loss alone Design B is best (1.6 MW) with Design C a close second (3.0 MW) and Design A far worse. Considering cost and practicality as well, Design B, a high-voltage transmission line with step-up and step-down transformers, is the best way to transmit the power.

content.alt_text: Toy bird launched from a slope at the foot of a vertical cliff 34 m high, with a wooden building on top, 45 m horizontally from the launch point. Not to scale.

content.text: Calculate the magnitude of the required launch velocity such that the toy bird strikes the base of the wooden building at the top of the cliff, 34 m above the launch height.
You know where the bird lands but not how long it takes, so write two equations, one for the horizontal distance and one for the vertical height, and eliminate $t$ between them.
The horizontal equation $x = u\cos 60^{\circ} \times t$ gives you a value for the product $ut$; substitute that product into the vertical equation $y = u\sin 60^{\circ} \times t - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}$.

Solve the vertical equation for $t$ first, then recover $u$ from the horizontal equation. As a check, $u$ must be greater than the speed needed to rise $34\,\mathrm{m}$ on its own, and the bird must still be climbing or at its peak when it arrives.

Horizontal: $45 = u\cos 60^\circ \times t = 0.5ut$, so $ut = 90$.
Vertical: $34 = u\sin 60^\circ \times t - \frac12 \times 9.8 \times t^{2} = 0.866 \times 90 - 4.9t^{2}$.
So $34 = 77.94 - 4.9t^{2}$, giving $t^{2} = 8.97$ and $t = 2.99\,\mathrm{s}$.
Hence $u = 90/2.99 = 30.1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so the required launch velocity is approximately $30\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

content.text: Outline ONE piece of evidence supporting Einstein's theory of relativity.
Choose an observation that has actually been measured: something involving muons, the speed of light, clocks flown on aircraft, or the fringes from Michelson-Morley.
The two marks are one for naming the evidence and one for linking it to what the theory predicts, so write both halves of that link in your answer.
The increased lifetime of muons created in the upper atmosphere and detected at ground level; time dilation predicts they live long enough to travel many kilometres at close to the speed of light.

Muons are created when cosmic rays strike the upper atmosphere, about 10 km above the ground. They travel at close to the speed of light and many are detected at ground level. In the muon's own rest frame the atmosphere is length contracted, so the muons reach the ground. In the ground frame time dilation means the muon lifetime is extended by $1/\sqrt{1-v^{2}/c^{2}}$, consistent with the observed lifetimes. This agreement with a relativistic prediction supports the theory.

content.text: What criteria are used to test and validate a theory?
Start with the strongest test: does the theory make quantitative predictions, and do controlled, repeated experiments agree with them to within experimental uncertainty?
Then consider the other criteria examiners accept, such as internal and mathematical consistency, and whether the theory explains and predicts phenomena that were not known when it was proposed.
Three distinct criteria earn the three marks, so avoid restating a single idea in different words. Agreement from several independent experiments is the strongest evidence of all.

A theory is tested by comparing its quantitative predictions with controlled experimental observations; it must be internally consistent and must be able to predict new phenomena that are then observed.

A theory is valid if its predictions agree, within experimental uncertainty, with repeated controlled experiments and observations; if it is mathematically self-consistent and not contradicted by other accepted theory; if it explains and predicts new phenomena that are subsequently detected; and if it is testable, general and economical in its assumptions. Evidence from independent experiments that all support the same predictions is the strongest test.

content.text: The distance between the cathode and screen in a cathode ray tube is 40 cm. If an electron travels through the tube at $3.0 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, what is the apparent distance from the cathode to the screen in the electron's frame of reference?
The separation is measured along the direction of the electron's motion, so the relevant effect is length contraction: $l = l_{0}\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}$.
Substitute the speed as a fraction of $c$ first. The answer then follows from a square root that is close to 1, so expect only a small change from $40\,\mathrm{cm}$.
Check the direction of the effect: length contraction can only shorten the distance, never lengthen it.
$l = 0.398\,\mathrm{m}$ (about 40 cm)

$l = l_0\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}} = 0.40\times\sqrt{1 - (3.0 \times 10^{7}/3.00 \times 10^{8})^{2}} = 0.40\times\sqrt{1 - 0.01} = 0.40 \times 0.995 = 0.398\,\mathrm{m}$, about 40 cm. Because the electron is moving at only one tenth of the speed of light, the length contraction is very small, so the apparent distance is almost unchanged.

content.text: How is the motor effect used to produce different sounds in a loudspeaker? Include a labelled diagram.

An alternating current in the voice coil in the field of the permanent magnet produces a force that reverses each half cycle, so the cone vibrates at the frequency of the current and sets the air oscillating; a larger current amplitude gives a larger force and a louder sound.

A loudspeaker contains a powerful permanent magnet with a cylindrical pole piece. A light copper voice coil is suspended in the annular gap so that the field passes across the coil. As the current alternates the force reverses, so the coil and the attached cone move back and forth. A frequency of 1000 Hz in the input produces 1000 oscillations per second of the cone and a note of pitch 1000 Hz. A larger current amplitude gives a larger force and a greater amplitude of cone vibration, compressing more air and producing a louder sound. The labelled diagram should show the permanent magnet, the pole piece, the voice coil, the cone, the diaphragm and the input terminals, with the direction of the magnetic field and of the current.

content.text: Why do the paths curve in different directions?
The field, the speed and the point of entry are all the same for the two particles, so the only quantity in $F = qvB$ that can differ between them is the sign of the charge.
Ask which quantity in that equation can be negative, and how a change in its sign reverses the direction of the force.
The two particles carry charges of opposite sign, so the magnetic force $F = qvB$ acts on them in opposite directions and they curve opposite ways.

The magnetic force on a moving charge is $F = qvB\sin\theta$. The two particles are travelling at the same speed through the same field, but they carry charges of opposite sign, so the force, and hence the direction of curvature, is reversed. Path P curves upwards and Path Q downwards.

items: 1 mark: identifies that the two particles carry opposite charges, so the magnetic force on them is in opposite directions.

content.text: Why are the paths circular?
Ask what the magnetic force does to the speed. It is always at right angles to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed cannot change.

Then ask what a constant, non-zero force of fixed magnitude, always perpendicular to the velocity, does to the direction of travel. That is the definition of uniform circular motion, which is why the paths are circular arcs rather than spirals.
Use the fact that the field is uniform: that is what makes the size of the force, and so the radius, constant.

The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes only the direction of the velocity, not its magnitude. It acts as a centripetal force and, because the field is uniform, it is constant, so the path is circular.

The force on a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field is always perpendicular to the velocity. It does no work, so the speed and the kinetic energy are constant. Because the field is uniform the force has constant magnitude $qvB$, and it is directed towards the centre of curvature, so it acts as a constant centripetal force and the path is a circle.

content.text: How do the properties of a particle affect the radius of curvature of its path in a uniform magnetic field?
Two forces must be equated: the magnetic force $qvB$ and the centripetal force $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$.
Set them equal and cancel one factor of $v$ before you read off how the radius depends on the mass, the speed, the charge and the field strength.
Check the sense of each dependence: a heavier or faster particle bends less sharply through the same field, so it must trace a wider circle.

$r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$. The radius is proportional to the mass and the speed and inversely proportional to the size of the charge; a faster or more massive particle follows a path of larger radius, while a particle with a larger charge follows a path of smaller radius.

Equating the magnetic force to the centripetal force, $qvB = mv^{2}/r$, gives $r = mv/qB$. For a fixed field strength the radius increases linearly with the mass of the particle and with its speed, and decreases as the magnitude of the charge increases. A negatively charged particle of the same mass and speed follows a path of the same radius as a positive one but curving the opposite way.

content.text: Why does Earth's magnetic field change over time?

(i) The field is not produced by a permanently magnetised body. Identify what is actually moving, and carrying current, inside the Earth, then note that this motion is not the same at all times or in all places.

(ii) Judge the bar-magnet drawing as a model of a field, not as a statement of fact. Check the direction convention on the field lines it shows, check how the real field is tilted relative to the axis of rotation, and check whether a permanently magnetised bar of iron could exist at the temperatures inside the Earth.

The field is produced by convection currents in the liquid conducting outer core. The pattern, speed and direction of this flow change with time, so the current and hence the field it produces also change, causing the field to drift and to reverse polarity from time to time.

The outer core is liquid iron, an electrical conductor. The temperature difference between the inner and outer core drives convection, and the movement of ionised iron constitutes a current. Since the distribution, speed and direction of these convection currents are not constant, the field they produce changes with time. Over geological time the field has reversed polarity many times, which is recorded in the magnetised rocks of the sea floor.

content.text: Data obtained from a shot-geophone analysis is shown on the following graph.

Read the axes first: time for signal arrival against distance from the shot, plotted to both sides of the shot. On a graph like this the gradient of each line is the reciprocal of the velocity of the path the signal actually took.

One line passes through the origin and the other does not. A non-zero intercept time on the time axis tells you the signal has had to travel down to a boundary between layers and back up to the surface before its travel through the top layer can begin.
For each line, say which path the signal followed and what its gradient therefore means - do not stop at describing the shape of the line.

C1 is the direct wave: it travels through the uppermost layer along the ground, so travel time is directly proportional to distance, its gradient is $1/v_1$ for that layer, and it passes through the origin. C2 is the head wave: it travels obliquely down to a faster, deeper layer, along that layer and back up to the surface, so its gradient is smaller, $1/v_2$ with $v_2 > v_1$, and it intercepts the time axis at a non-zero intercept time, the time taken to reach the interface and return. C2 therefore arrives before C1 at the larger distances plotted.

In a shot-geophone (seismic refraction) survey the travel time of a signal is plotted against the distance from the shot, in both directions. C1 is the direct wave travelling along the ground surface through the uppermost layer, so travel time is directly proportional to distance and it plots as a straight line through the origin with gradient $1/v_1$. C2 is the head wave, which travels obliquely down to a faster, deeper layer, along that layer and back up to the surface; its smaller gradient means the lines cross at the critical distance, and its positive intercept (the intercept time) on the time axis gives the depth of the deeper layer. The symmetry of the two branches about the shot shows the layers are horizontal and laterally uniform.

content.text: Other than the geometric fit of continents or magnetic evidence, what evidence supports the theory of plate tectonics?

Earthquakes, volcanoes and deep ocean trenches are concentrated along plate boundaries rather than randomly, and the age of the ocean floor increases with distance from the ridges, showing that plates move and are created and destroyed at their edges.

Independent evidence includes: (i) earthquakes, volcanoes and deep trenches concentrated in narrow zones along plate boundaries, including the circum-Pacific belt and the mid-ocean ridges, rather than randomly distributed; (ii) the age of ocean floor rock increasing with distance from the ridge, so ocean crust is young and is being created at ridges; (iii) the continental shelves and the rock formations, fossils and glacial deposits of continents once joined matching across ocean basins; (iv) modern GPS and laser measurements showing plates moving at the predicted rates; and (v) the distribution and depth of ocean trenches and the pattern of deep-focus earthquakes identifying the subduction zones where oceanic crust is consumed.

content.text: How is remote sensing used to obtain information about Earth?

Sort the instruments into two families: those that simply record radiation arriving from the Earth, and those that send out a pulse of their own and time the echo. Passive and active is the usual terminology.
For each family name one instrument and the physics it relies on - emission and reflection for passive, the speed of the wave and the inverse square law for active.
Then give the trade-off that decides where a satellite goes: how much ground it can cover against how much detail it can resolve. This is the kind of limitation the question is looking for.

Satellites carry instruments that detect electromagnetic radiation. Passive sensors record radiation emitted or reflected by the Earth's surface; active sensors such as radar and lidar send out their own pulses and time the echoes. This is used for mapping, weather, mineral exploration and monitoring the environment.

Remote sensing obtains information about the Earth without physical contact. A satellite carries a sensor on a platform above the Earth. In passive remote sensing the sensor simply records radiation arriving from the Earth: visible and infrared photographic cameras record reflected sunlight, and thermal infrared radiometers record the surface emission, which by Stefan's law and Wien's law reveals surface temperature; microwave radiometers record emission at longer wavelengths, penetrating cloud. In active remote sensing the instrument sends out its own radiation, usually radar or laser pulses, and measures the time taken for the echo to return, giving surface height, while the intensity of the echo depends on surface roughness, moisture and dielectric constant; synthetic aperture radar gives day and night images. The Doppler shift of the returned wave is used to measure surface wind speed and ocean currents. A trade-off exists between spatial resolution and area covered: detailed high resolution images are obtained from low orbits with a narrow swath, while wide coverage of poorer resolution comes from high orbits. Applications include crop and forest mapping, mineral and oil exploration from the surface signature of rocks, weather forecasting from cloud images, monitoring sea level rise, the hole in the ozone layer, bushfires, floods and urban growth.

content.text: The first X-ray image of a human was made in 1895 but it was not until 1972 that CAT scan imaging was developed.
The 77-year gap is a gap in technology, not in physics. Identify the step a plain radiograph does not need but a CAT scan does, and then ask what had to be invented before that step was practical.
For the PET and CAT contrasts keep two questions apart: what information the image carries, and where the radiation is produced. Answering both for each modality avoids the usual confusion.

When you write about the 20th century developments, be specific about what each one contributed - processing speed, memory, storage, display, detector quality - rather than simply saying 'computers were invented'.

items: (i) The gap is a gap in data handling, not in physics. A plain radiograph is a single exposure of the whole body and needed no computation, but a CAT scan records hundreds of narrow-beam projections and must reconstruct them mathematically into an image of a single slice. Handling that much data by complex algorithms required computers that were not cheap or widely available before the microchip computers of the 1970s, so CAT scanning had to wait until 1972.

(ii) A CAT scan is structural: it images anatomy, giving the shape, size, position and X-ray density of bones, organs, blood vessels and lesions, with a spatial resolution of about $1\,\mathrm{mm}$ and a scan time of seconds. A PET scan is functional: it maps where a radioactive tracer is taken up, so it shows the metabolic or physiological activity of tissue, with a hot spot marking a tumour or inflammation; its spatial resolution is only a few millimetres and it is slower and more expensive.

(iii) In CAT the radiation is made in the machine: electrons are accelerated across a high voltage and decelerated on a tungsten target, producing X-rays by bremsstrahlung together with characteristic X-rays, which are then fired through the patient. In PET the radiation is made inside the body: an injected radionuclide such as F-18 decays, the positrons annihilate with electrons in the tissue and each annihilation produces two gamma photons of $511\,\mathrm{keV}$ travelling in opposite directions, which are detected in coincidence.

content.text: A conventional radiograph is a single shadow projection and required no computation beyond recording the film. A CAT (computed axial tomography) scan rotates a narrow X-ray beam around the patient, recording hundreds of projections, and then reconstructs the distribution of X-ray attenuation into an image of one thin slice. This required large numbers of measurements, fast accurate detectors, algorithms for image reconstruction and computers able to perform many millions of operations and to store the data. Computer technology of 1895 could not do this; the development of transistors, integrated circuits, fast mainframe computers and then minicomputers through the 1950s to 1970s, together with improved X-ray tubes and detectors, allowed the first practical CAT scanner in 1972. The 77-year interval is therefore explained by the essential dependence of CAT scanning on computing power.

For (a)(ii) the cleanest contrast is what each scan measures. CAT records X-ray attenuation, so it returns a map of density and therefore a map of anatomy; PET records the coincidence gamma pairs from an injected tracer, so it returns a map of tracer uptake and therefore a map of function. That is why a lesion is commonly located with PET and then imaged in detail with CAT.

For (a)(iii) the contrast that carries the marks is where the radiation is made. Both modalities detect photons outside the body, but the CAT scanner generates its own X-rays in a tube outside the patient, while the PET scanner generates no radiation in the machine at all: the gamma rays are produced inside the body when positrons from the injected radionuclide annihilate with electrons, giving two $511\,\mathrm{keV}$ photons per event travelling back to back, which is why the detectors are arranged in rings and only count events seen in coincidence.

content.text: What effects do the pulses of radio waves have on hydrogen nuclei in the body of a person having a magnetic resonance image scan?

In the strong static field the hydrogen nuclei line up with the field, producing a small net magnetisation. Ask what a radio wave at exactly the right frequency does to that arrangement, and what the nuclei do immediately afterwards.
The image is built from signals the nuclei themselves give out on the way back to equilibrium, so describe the whole cycle in order: align, disturb, precess, relax, emit.
For the second half, name the 20th century physics behind each ingredient separately - the source of the strong field, and the machinery that turns a large volume of measured data into an image.

items: (i) The hydrogen nuclei have magnetic moments. In the strong field of the scanner they align with the field (some against it), so there is a small net magnetisation along the field. A pulse of radio waves at the Larmor frequency, applied perpendicular to the field, is absorbed by the precessing nuclei and tips the net magnetisation out of alignment, flipping some of them into a higher energy level. When the pulse ends the nuclei precess about the field direction and relax back towards it, and as they do so they emit radio waves at the Larmor frequency; those emitted signals are detected and used to form the image.

(ii) Nuclear magnetic resonance was discovered in 1946 by Bloch and Purcell, which showed that the resonance of hydrogen nuclei in a magnetic field could be measured and used to locate and identify them, so the physics existed before the scanner. Two later advances made MRI possible: superconducting magnets, which produce the very strong, homogeneous and stable fields a scanner needs, and the transistor and integrated circuit, whose microchips gave computers fast enough to acquire the weak signals from the detectors and Fourier-transform them into an image in a clinically acceptable time. Radio frequency and gradient coil technology, based on the physics of oscillating fields and of nuclear spin resonance, then produced the first whole-body MRI scanners.

content.text: The scanner's main magnetic field causes the magnetic moments of the hydrogen nuclei to align with the field, producing a small net magnetisation along the field. A short pulse of radio waves at the Larmor frequency is applied perpendicular to the field. Its oscillating magnetic field is absorbed by the proton spins, tipping the net magnetisation away from the direction of the main field. Immediately after the pulse the nuclei precess about the main field direction at the Larmor frequency $f_0 = \gamma B/2\pi$ and, as the spins relax back towards equilibrium, they emit radio waves at the same frequency. A gradient in the field encodes position in the frequency and phase, and a computer combines the signals into an image.

For (b)(ii) the answer needs two ingredients, the physics and the technology. The physics ingredient is the discovery of nuclear magnetic resonance itself (Bloch and Purcell, 1946) and the measurement of the resonance frequency of hydrogen nuclei in a known field, which is what identifies the hydrogen in a sample. The technology ingredients are superconducting magnets, needed because MRI requires fields of a few tesla that could not be produced economically before the 1960s, and semiconductor electronics, which gave both the fast linear electronics and the computers needed to Fourier-transform a very large volume of weak data into an image.

content.text: Describe the properties that make a radioactive isotope useful for medical imaging. Include a specific example of a radioactive isotope in your answer.

There are three separate requirements, and you need all three: the radiation must be able to get out of the body and be detected outside it, the half-life must suit the time the scan takes, and the element must be chemically able to be put where you want it to go.

Then give a named isotope with its half-life and its use, and say why that half-life is the right one for that particular job - too short and the tracer decays before the scan, too long and the patient is irradiated for no reason.

It must emit radiation that can escape the body and be detected, have a suitable half-life, and be able to be taken up selectively by the organ of interest. Technetium-99m is used for bone scans: it emits 140 keV gamma rays with a 6 hour half-life and is taken up by the bone.

Useful properties include: the type of radiation must be able to leave the body and be detected outside it, so gamma rays (or, for PET, positrons) are used rather than alpha or most beta radiation; the energy must be high enough to penetrate the body but low enough to give a reasonable dose; the half-life must be long enough for the isotope to be produced, transported, incorporated into a tracer and used in a scan (hours or days) but short enough that most of it decays away afterwards, minimising the patient's dose and the hazard of contamination; it must be chemically able to be incorporated into a compound that concentrates in the organ of interest; and it must be produced in sufficient quantity at reasonable cost. Example: technetium-99m, a gamma emitter with a 6 hour half-life, is injected as technetium MDP and taken up preferentially by actively growing bone, so areas of abnormal bone turnover show up on the scan. Other examples are iodine-131 (8 day half-life) concentrated by the thyroid, thallium-201 for heart muscle and F-18 (110 minute half-life) for PET.

content.text: Explain how endoscopes obtain images of internal organs.

One piece of physics does all the work here: light is trapped inside a fibre by repeated total internal reflection at the boundary between the glass core and the cladding, so it can follow a bundle round corners inside the body.
Then work out why one bundle of fibres is enough to light the organ while the other has to preserve the image, and what the arrangement of the fibres in each bundle must guarantee for that to work.

A flexible bundle of optical fibres is passed into the body. One incoherent bundle carries light down to the tip by total internal reflection to illuminate the organ, and a second coherent bundle returns the image of the organ by the same process to an eyepiece or camera, giving a real-time view.

An endoscope contains two bundles of very fine optical fibres sealed in a flexible, steerable tube. The fibre optic light guide, an incoherent bundle in which the fibres are randomly arranged, carries light from a strong external source down to the distal tip, where a lens or prism spreads it over the organ. An objective lens at the tip forms a real image of the organ, and a second, coherent bundle, in which each fibre is in the same position at both ends, carries each point of the image back along the bundle to the eyepiece, where the pattern of illuminated fibres reproduces the image. Light is confined within each fibre by repeated total internal reflection at the glass-air interface between the core and the cladding, so it can travel round corners over a metre or more. A jet of air or water, or a laser, may also be used to clear the view.

content.text: Discuss the range of information obtained from, and the limitations of, ultrasound medical imaging technology.
Take the range of information first and the limitations second, and do not let them run together - a limitation only has meaning once the reader knows what the scan can do.
For the limitations, remember that ultrasound is a mechanical wave: the resolution is set by its wavelength, and it needs a medium to travel in, which is why a gas-filled cavity and bone defeat it.
Include the advantages as well - no ionising radiation and a real-time image - because a 'limitations' mark usually expects the comparison with the alternatives.

Ultrasound gives real-time cross-sectional images of internal organs, their size, shape and position, the growth and development of a fetus, and abnormalities such as gallstones, cysts and tumours; Doppler ultrasound also gives the direction and speed of blood flow. It uses sound rather than ionising radiation, so it is safe, especially in pregnancy. Limitations are that the resolution is set by the sound wavelength, so small structures cannot be resolved; sound cannot cross air or bone, so lungs, bowel gas and the adult brain cannot be imaged; reflections and shadowing degrade the image; a coupling medium is needed; and operator skill and cost limit its use.

Information obtained: the reflected sound is converted into a cross-sectional image showing the position, size and shape of internal organs and the boundaries between them, so growth, the stage of a pregnancy, the position of the fetus and the presence of cysts, tumours, stones, aneurysms or fluid can be assessed. Because the image is produced in real time, moving structures such as the heart valves can be watched working. In Doppler mode the frequency shift of the echo is used to measure the speed and direction of blood flow, so valve disease, blocked vessels and the rate and direction of flow can be assessed. No ionising radiation is used, so it is safe for an unborn child and can be repeated frequently, and it is cheap and portable compared with X-rays and MRI.\nLimitations: the resolution is set by the wavelength of the sound, about 1 mm for the frequencies used, so structures smaller than a few millimetres, such as cells, cannot be resolved and the image is granular. Ultrasound cannot travel through air or bone, so gas-filled lungs and bowel produce bright echoes and shadowing and cannot be examined, and the adult brain and the limbs cannot be scanned through bone, although ultrasound is used through the fontanelle in babies. Bone, calcification, metal and gas reflect almost all the sound, so structures beyond them are hidden. Reverberation and acoustic shadowing from curved surfaces cause artefacts. A coupling gel or water bath is needed to transmit the sound into the body, the results depend on the skill of the operator, the equipment is expensive, and a gas-filled body region cannot be imaged at all.

content.text: Why do astronomers use both apparent and absolute measurements in photometry?

Apparent brightness is what actually arrives at the telescope; absolute brightness is what would arrive if the star were placed at a standard distance. Ask what extra variable apparent brightness folds in that absolute brightness removes.

For the second half, do not confuse the two techniques: one measures the total light arriving from the star, the other sorts that light by wavelength before measuring it. Then say what each can tell you that the other cannot.
Apparent brightness also depends on distance, so absolute measurements are used to compare stars fairly and to determine their true luminosities.

The brightness a star appears to have depends on how much light it emits and on how far away it is, following the inverse square law, so a nearby dim star can look brighter than a distant luminous one. An absolute magnitude removes the distance effect, so astronomers can compare the intrinsic luminosities of stars and place them correctly on a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, while the apparent magnitude still tells them how bright the star looks from Earth and, with the absolute magnitude, how far away it is.

content.text: Describe the problems associated with ground-based optical astronomy in terms of resolution.
There are two independent limits on the resolution of a telescope, and only one of them responds to building a bigger instrument. Identify both before deciding which one governs in practice.
Compare them numerically in order of magnitude - one improves as the aperture grows and the other does not, and that comparison is the heart of the answer.

Then treat loss of contrast as a separate problem from loss of resolution: the sky's own light, from airglow, light pollution and the daytime sky, raises the background and hides faint objects even when the resolution is good.

Turbulence in the atmosphere distorts the incoming wavefront, blurring the image and limiting the resolution to about 1 arcsecond, whatever the size of the telescope. Sky glow, light pollution and the scattered and thermal light of the atmosphere reduce the contrast so faint objects cannot be seen.

Two separate limits apply. The first is the diffraction limit of the instrument, $\theta = 1.22\lambda/D$, which improves as the aperture increases. The second, and the dominant one for a ground-based telescope, is atmospheric seeing: the Earth's atmosphere is turbulent, so the wavefront is constantly distorted and the image of a point source is spread into a seeing disc of about one arcsecond. Increasing the aperture does not reduce this, so no ground-based optical telescope can do better than about 0.5 to 1 arcsecond, whereas a space telescope in the ultraviolet is limited only by diffraction. In addition, the atmosphere scatters and emits light: airglow, light pollution from cities and zodiacal light raise the sky background and reduce the contrast, so faint objects such as distant galaxies and faint stars are lost in the glare; the thermal emission of the atmosphere also blocks much of the infrared; and the daytime sky is far brighter than the objects of interest.

content.text: Draw a flow diagram for stellar evolution using the following celestial objects: Black hole; Main sequence star; Neutron star/pulsar; Planetary nebula; Red giant; Supernova; White dwarf. Your flow diagram must include all of the objects listed above.
Every star starts the same way; what differs is the mass, and mass decides what happens after the core has run out of fuel.

Sketch the common trunk first, then add the branches. Two branches are needed because the objects on the list include alternatives to each other - a neutron star and a black hole cannot both lie on a single path.

Decide what the core becomes once it can no longer release energy by fusion; that single step is what splits your diagram in two, and where the masses of the branches differ is what decides the final remnant.

Main sequence star $\rightarrow$ red giant $\rightarrow$ planetary nebula $\rightarrow$ white dwarf (low mass); or main sequence star $\rightarrow$ red giant $\rightarrow$ supernova $\rightarrow$ neutron star/pulsar or black hole (high mass).

The flow diagram has a common beginning and then two branches. All stars begin on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen in their cores. When the core hydrogen is exhausted a star leaves the main sequence and becomes a red giant, fusing hydrogen in a shell around a degenerate helium core. What happens next depends on the mass. For a star of about the Sun's mass or less, the core fuses helium to carbon and oxygen; the star then sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula and the hot exposed core cools as a white dwarf. For a star of more than about eight solar masses, the core fuses successively to iron; once the core is iron it cannot release further energy, so the core collapses in a supernova. The remnant is a neutron star (a pulsar if it spins and its beams are seen) if the core mass is below about three solar masses, or a black hole if it is above, in which case the black hole is added to the diagram as an alternative to the neutron star.

content.text: Explain how trigonometric parallax is used to determine the distances to stars.

Parallax needs a baseline that is large compared with the distance being measured, so ask where on Earth you could put the telescope to make that baseline as long as possible, and how long you would have to wait.
Then relate the small angle you measure to the distance with $p = b/d$, and take care with the factor of two between the total apparent shift and the parallax angle itself.
The convenient result is $d(\mathrm{pc}) = 1/p(\mathrm{arcsec})$. Check your units are consistent before substituting, and think about why this method stops working for distant stars.

The star's position is measured against distant background stars from two places on opposite sides of Earth's orbit, six months apart. The small shift in its apparent position is the parallax angle. For a baseline of $2\,\mathrm{AU}$ the distance in parsecs is one divided by the parallax angle in arcseconds.

The stars are so distant that the Earth appears to orbit about a very small circle compared with their distances. Nevertheless, from opposite sides of Earth's orbit a nearby star appears to shift slightly against the pattern of distant background stars. The apparent position of the star is measured on photographic plates taken six months apart, and the total shift is halved to give the parallax angle $p$, the angle subtended at the star by the radius of Earth's orbit, so the baseline is $2\,\mathrm{AU}$ or $3.0 \times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$. Since $p$ is extremely small, $d = b/\tan p \approx b/p$. Expressed in convenient units, $d(\,\mathrm{pc}) = 1/p(\,\mathrm{arcsec})$: a star with a parallax of 0.1 arcsecond is 10 parsecs away.

content.text: Analyse the above data to write a detailed description of this binary system.
Take the table first: divide the two luminosities to get how unequal the stars are, and subtract the apparent magnitudes to see how much brighter the brighter star looks from Earth.

Then place each star on the H-R diagram. A spectral class fixes the surface temperature, but a star is only on the main sequence if its luminosity is the one expected for that class - work out which of these two does.

For the period, measure the spacing of the repeating dips on the light curve, and remember that two different depths mean the two stars are eclipsing each other in turn. Finally, put the average separation and that period into $M = 4\pi^{2}a^{3}/GT^{2}$ for the total mass of the system.

The system is a wide, unequal, detached eclipsing binary with an orbital period of about $40$ years and an average separation of $2.2 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{km}$. The light curve shows two distinct minima in each cycle - deep minima near years 9 and 50 and shallower minima near years 27 and 70 - so each star passes in front of the other in turn and the stars are separate bodies rather than in contact. Star A has an apparent magnitude of $0.34$, a spectral class of F5 and a luminosity $7.3$ times the Sun's, so it is an ordinary main sequence star slightly hotter and more luminous than the Sun. Star B, although its spectral class of A4 places it at a higher surface temperature than F5, has a luminosity of only $0.0063$ of the Sun's, so on the H-R diagram it lies far below the main sequence for its class and must be a much smaller object such as a white dwarf. Star A is over a thousand times more luminous than Star B, $7.3/0.0063 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{3}$, and their apparent magnitudes differ by $13.16 - 0.34 = 12.8$, so almost all the light of the system comes from Star A. The total mass of the system is about $3.9 \times 10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$, that is about $2.0$ solar masses, so almost all of the mass is in Star A as well.

Period. The deep minima near years 9 and 50 are about $40$ years apart, and the shallow minima near years 27 and 70 are the secondary eclipses, about $20$ years after the primary. The two repeat together, so the orbital period of the binary is $T \approx 40$ years.

Nature of the system. The brightness drops are narrow and regular, so they are eclipses, and two minima occur in each cycle at different depths, so each star passes in front of the other in turn. The system is therefore a detached eclipsing binary, not a contact binary.

The stars. Dividing the two luminosities, $7.3/0.0063 = 1.16 \times 10^{3}$, and subtracting the apparent magnitudes, $13.16 - 0.34 = 12.8$, shows how unequal the two stars are. On the H-R diagram Star A, an F5 star at about seven times the Sun's luminosity, lies on the upper main sequence just hotter and more luminous than the Sun. Star B's spectral class of A4 places it at a higher surface temperature than F5, yet its luminosity is only $0.0063$ of the Sun's, far below the main sequence value for that class; it must therefore be a much smaller object than a normal A4 main sequence star, consistent with a white dwarf, and it contributes very little light to the system.

content.text: Using diagrams and text, outline Bohr's explanation of the Balmer series.

Begin from Bohr's two postulates: the electron may occupy only certain allowed orbits, each with a fixed energy, and it neither radiates while in an orbit nor changes energy without absorbing or emitting a photon.
Conservation of energy then fixes the photon: $hf = E_i - E_f$. Work out which initial and final states produce the visible lines, and say why the series is called the Balmer series.

The diagram is part of the answer: draw the nucleus with a few labelled orbits and arrows for every transition that ends in $n = 2$, then combine $E = hf$ with $c = f\lambda$ to show that the wavelengths are discrete and crowd together towards the short-wavelength limit.

In the Bohr model the electron orbits the nucleus only in certain fixed energy states. When an electron falls from a state with $n \ge 3$ to the state with $n = 2$ it emits a photon of energy $E_i - E_f$, so the visible lines of the Balmer series are emitted; since only certain transitions are allowed, only certain wavelengths appear.

Bohr proposed that the electron can occupy only certain allowed orbits, each with a fixed total energy $E_n = -13.6/n^{2}\,\mathrm{eV}$ for hydrogen, and that it neither radiates while in an orbit nor changes energy without absorbing or emitting a photon. A hydrogen atom is excited to a higher level by absorbing a photon of exactly the right energy, or in a discharge tube by collisions. When it falls back it emits a single photon, and by conservation of energy $E = hf = E_i - E_f$, so $hf = E_i - E_f$. The Balmer series consists of the lines produced by all transitions that end in the $n = 2$ state, that is from $n = 3, 4, 5 \ldots$; the $n = 1$ series is in the ultraviolet. Combining $E = hf$ with $c = f\lambda$ and the energy levels gives Rydberg's formula $1/\lambda = R(1/n_f^{2} - 1/n_i^{2})$, with $n_f = 2$ for the Balmer series, so the wavelengths are determined by the initial level alone and a series of discrete lines, crowded towards the short wavelength limit, is produced rather than a continuous spectrum.

content.text: What are the requirements for an uncontrolled nuclear chain reaction, and how does the equivalence between mass and energy relate to what occurs during the natural radioactivity process?

Work through the chain-reaction conditions one at a time: the fuel must be able to absorb a neutron and split, and each split must release enough free neutrons to keep the neutron population growing rather than shrinking.

Ask what would happen if neutrons leaked out of the fuel or were absorbed by impurities - that is what sets the quantity and purity conditions, and it is why a moderator is not required in the fast chain reaction.

For the radioactivity half, compare the mass of the parent nucleus with the total mass of the daughter nucleus and the emitted particles. A difference in mass is not a violation of anything: by $E = \Delta m c^{2}$ it is energy.

Uncontrolled chain reaction: a fissile fuel such as U-235, more than one neutron released per fission, and enough fuel of sufficient purity that neutrons are not lost; a moderator is not required. Radioactivity: the products have a total mass less than the parent nucleus, and the missing mass $\Delta m$ is released as energy $\Delta E = \Delta m c^{2}$, so mass-energy as a whole is conserved but mass alone is not.

Uncontrolled chain reaction. The fuel must be fissile, that is able to absorb a neutron and split; U-235 and Pu-239 are the important ones. Each fission must release at least one neutron, so that each neutron absorbed can produce several further fissions. The quantity of fuel must be large enough and pure enough that few neutrons are lost by leakage or absorbed by impurities, so that on average more than one neutron from each fission causes a further fission and the number of neutrons grows. No moderator is essential, because the fast neutrons from a fission can themselves cause further fission of U-235.\nRadioactivity. The daughter nucleus and the emitted alpha or beta particle have a combined mass less than that of the original nucleus. This mass defect arises because the products are more tightly bound, and the missing mass appears as kinetic energy of the products and as energy carried away by gamma radiation. Einstein's relation $E = mc^{2}$ means that mass is a form of energy, so the law of conservation of mass and the law of conservation of energy are replaced by a single law of conservation of mass-energy, and it is this law that must be applied to every decay equation.

content.text: How can neutrons be used to probe the positions of nuclei within the structure of a metal crystal? Make reference to the work of Louis de Broglie in your answer.

Neutrons carry no charge, so they are not deflected by the electron cloud. A neutron beam is therefore scattered almost entirely by the nuclei - which is what makes it a probe of nuclear positions rather than of electron structure.

Now use de Broglie: choose the neutron's speed so that its wavelength is comparable with the spacing of the atomic planes, and regularly spaced nuclei will diffract the beam just as a diffraction grating does.
The measurement to make is the angle at which the diffracted beams appear, and the quantity it gives you is the separation of the planes. Say explicitly how you get from the angle to the spacing.

De Broglie showed that a neutron of suitable velocity has a wavelength comparable with the spacing of the atomic planes in a crystal. The neutrons diffract from these planes, and measuring the diffraction angles gives the spacing and arrangement of the nuclei.

De Broglie's matter-wave hypothesis, later confirmed by electron diffraction, shows that any particle of momentum $p$ behaves as a wave of wavelength $\lambda = h/p = h/mv$. Neutrons are uncharged, so they penetrate deeply into matter and interact only weakly with the electron cloud, which means a neutron beam is scattered mainly by the regularly spaced nuclei in a metal crystal. By choosing the neutron velocity so that the de Broglie wavelength is comparable with the spacing of the atomic planes, the neutrons are diffracted by the planes, just as X-rays are, and a diffraction pattern is observed. Measuring the angles at which the diffracted beams appear, using the Bragg relation, gives the separation of the planes and hence the positions of the nuclei, and the intensities of the diffracted beams show how many nuclei lie in each plane. Neutron diffraction is therefore used to map the arrangement of nuclei in metals, magnetic structures and large biological molecules.

content.text: Explain how the internal structures of the proton and neutron determine their properties.

Write down the quark composition of each nucleon, then add up the quark charges using $+\frac{2e}{3}$ for an up quark and $-\frac{e}{3}$ for a down quark. The totals explain why one nucleon is charged and the other is not.

The fact that no fractional charge is ever observed is a separate statement about confinement, so keep it separate from the arithmetic. The near equality of the two masses is another property that needs explaining.

For the accelerator part, ask what an accelerator must do to the particles it fires and what the detectors record when those particles collide. The energies involved are not incidental - check what they have to be comparable with.

A proton is uud and a neutron is udd, held together by the strong force. The up quark has charge $+2e/3$ and the down quark $-e/3$, so the proton has charge $+e$ and the neutron is neutral, and no fractional charge is ever observed because quarks are confined.

In the quark model the proton is two up quarks and one down quark and the neutron is one up quark and two down quarks, bound by the strong force. Each up quark carries charge $+2e/3$ and each down quark $-e/3$, so a proton totals $+e$ and a neutron totals 0. Because quarks are confined, free fractional charges are never observed. The nucleon mass comes mostly from the energy of the confined quarks and gluons, so the different quark arrangements give the two particles their different charges, magnetic moments and stability.

content.text: Describe the role of conservation laws in the development of atomic physics.
Name the laws that every atomic and nuclear process must satisfy - there are several, and a 2 mark answer should list more than one.
Then give one concrete example of a discovery that came out of applying a law to data that did not add up, naming both the law and what was missing from the measurements.

Conservation of charge, mass-energy, baryon number and lepton number are used to check every decay and collision, to predict the existence of unobserved particles such as the neutrino, and to guide the development of atomic models.

Conservation laws are the constraints that every atomic and nuclear process must satisfy, and they have been central to the development of atomic physics. The law of conservation of charge shows that charge must be balanced in every decay and reaction, which immediately implies that electrons cannot change into protons and that a positron must be emitted whenever an electron is absorbed. The law of conservation of mass-energy, in which mass and energy are interconvertible through $E = mc^{2}$, allows mass to balance in nuclear reactions where the mass of the products is less than that of the reactants, and it is this law that gave the mass defect in beta decay the same status as energy. When the energy and momentum of the beta particles were measured and found not to balance, the conservation laws were not abandoned; instead the neutrino was predicted and then detected, which opened the way to the weak interaction. Conservation of baryon number restricted which reactions could occur and helped establish that protons and neutrons are the nucleons from which nuclei are built, and in quark models it explains why mesons cannot be produced alone. Conservation of lepton number, charm and strangeness has guided the discovery and classification of every new particle since, and the conservation laws remain the test that every proposed model of atomic and nuclear structure must pass.

content.text: Explain the use of relays, rather than transistors, to switch large currents in circuits.

Compare the two devices on two separate counts: who physically carries the large current, and whether the control circuit is electrically isolated from the load. Electrical isolation is the property a relay has and a transistor does not.

A relay's control circuit energises an electromagnet which moves a set of heavy, isolated contacts that carry the large current, so the switching is electrically isolated and the large current never passes through the control device. A transistor large enough to carry the current would be costly and easily damaged by the current and voltage surges.

A relay is an electromagnetic switch. A small control current through a few turns of wire creates a magnetic field in a soft iron core, which attracts an armature and closes a set of contacts that are electrically isolated from the control circuit and made of thick conducting material. The large current to be switched therefore flows only through these heavy contacts, which can be made to carry hundreds of amps, while the electronics that drives the coil handle only a small current and are completely protected from the high voltage and current of the load. A relay can therefore be operated by any controller, including a low-power logic circuit, timer or computer output. A transistor, by contrast, must itself carry the full current and withstand the full voltage across the load; to switch large currents a power transistor must be large and expensive, it dissipates significant power as heat, it is easily damaged by the inductive back emf or by a voltage or current surge when the load is switched, and it does not provide the electrical isolation between the control and load circuits that a relay does. Relays are therefore still used where large currents, high voltages or safety isolation are required, even though transistors are cheaper and smaller for small currents.

content.text: Analyse how the development of modern electronics has been influenced by our increased understanding of the properties of materials and the development of complex manufacturing techniques.

Plan this as three moves: the understanding of material properties that made the devices possible, the manufacturing techniques that made them ever smaller, faster and cheaper, and the consequences for society including at least one negative consequence or a balanced judgement. The marking guide allocates marks across all three.

Understanding of semiconductor band structure gave diodes, transistors, ICs, LEDs and solar cells, and better fabrication (photolithography, etching, CVD) made them ever smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable, so billions of components now fit on a chip, giving computers, mobile phones and modern medical technology; the cost is large volumes of electronic waste, resource consumption and energy use in manufacture.

Modern electronics exists because two things were understood and then engineered. First, the properties of materials. The band theory of solids showed that a semiconductor has a filled valence band and an empty conduction band separated by a small gap, and that the gap and the conductivity can be controlled by doping and by the number of electrons in each valence shell of the dopant. This understanding produced the rectifying diode, the p-n junction, the bipolar and field effect transistor, the integrated circuit, LEDs and semiconductor lasers, and photovoltaic cells; the ability to make p-type and n-type regions in the same crystal, and to join them to a third terminal, is what allows a transistor to act as a switch or to amplify. Knowledge of other materials extended this: superconductors give lossless power transmission and very strong MRI magnets, magnetic materials give data storage, and thin film and liquid crystal materials give displays and solar control.\nSecond, complex manufacturing techniques. The planar process, photoresist masking, photolithography, etching, ion implantation, chemical vapour deposition and oxidation, together with automated step-and-repeat mask aligners and clean-room air filtration, allow patterns of a few tens of nanometres to be repeated with great accuracy over a whole wafer. As the minimum feature size has fallen from about 10 micrometres in the 1970s to a few nanometres, the number of components on a single integrated circuit has risen from tens to billions, so processors, memory and sensors have become enormously faster, smaller, cheaper and more reliable, which is the trend described by Moore's law.\nAs a result electronics is now fundamental to society: computers and the internet, mobile phones, digital cameras, flat panel televisions, GPS, medical monitoring and implants, industrial control, aircraft and automobile systems, and space exploration. There are costs: the energy and ultrapure chemicals needed to manufacture chips, the mining of rare metals, the very short working life of devices which produces a large and growing volume of electronic waste that is difficult and expensive to recycle, and rapid obsolescence of older equipment. On balance the benefits greatly outweigh these costs, which are being reduced by longer-lived products, recycling and energy-efficient manufacturing.
